name: Marundeeswarar Temple, Thiruvanmiyur
deity: Shiva as Marundeeswarar (Palvannanathar), Lord of Medicine, with the goddess Tripurasundari
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Thondai Nadu, sung in the Tevaram by Appar and Sambandar (7th century); structural temple with Chola and later additions
dynasty: Pallava-era shrine, rebuilt and expanded under the Cholas, with later Vijayanagara additions
summary: Marundeeswarar, the Lord of Medicine, is the Shiva of Thiruvanmiyur on Chennai's coast, where Valmiki is said to have worshipped, Agastya learned the healing herbs and the divine cow Kamadhenu found release, praised in the Tevaram by Appar and Sambandar.

sections.history: Thiruvanmiyur, today a southern neighbourhood of Chennai on the East Coast Road, is one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams of Thondai Nadu, praised in the seventh century by two of the great Tevaram saints, Sambandar and Appar. Tradition derives its name from the sage Valmiki, the author of the Ramayana: the place was Thiruvalmikiyur, the town of Valmiki, which time wore down to Thiruvanmiyur. The age of the present temple is told differently in different accounts. Some speak of a Pallava-era shrine rebuilt in stone by the Cholas, with dates ranging from the ninth to the eleventh century, and later additions ascribed to the Vijayanagara period; one source records visits by Rajendra Chola I between 1012 and 1044. Whatever the exact chronology, the shrine is among the old anchors of the Chennai coast and still keeps pace with the life of the city.
sections.architecture: Gateway towers mark the temple: a seven-tiered rajagopuram on the east and a five-tiered gopuram on the west, the latter serving as the busiest entrance beside the bus terminus on the East Coast Road; accounts differ on the number and arrangement of the towers. The self-manifested linga of Marundeeswarar faces west, an uncommon orientation among Shiva temples. Within, a large mandapam of thirty-six carved pillars houses the Somaskanda form of Shiva. The goddess Tripurasundari has her shrine in the eastern outer prakaram, a shrine to the sage Valmiki stands on the western side, and the sacred Vanni tree, the sthala vriksha, grows within the precincts. A large temple tank completes the setting.
sections.legends: Many stories gather at Thiruvanmiyur, and nearly all of them return to healing. The first is of Agastya, the sage of the south, who stayed here and suffered a grievous pain in the stomach. Shiva appeared to him beneath the Vanni tree and taught him the virtues of herbs and plants, and from this the Lord is called Marundeeswarar, Lord of Medicine. The second is of Valmiki, who is said to have worshipped Shiva here and asked to remain; the town carries his name. The third is of Kamadhenu, the divine cow cursed by the sage Vasishta, who found release by worshipping the self-manifested linga. In one telling her milk whitened the linga, giving the Lord the name Palvannanathar, He of the colour of milk; in another she struck it with her hooves while fleeing captors, and the marks are said to be seen on the linga still. Tradition also links the linga to the lifting of a curse upon Indra.
sections.festivals: The great festival is the Panguni Brahmotsavam, held in March or April, when the deities go out in procession through the neighbourhood and a ceremony is kept beneath the Vanni tree on the ninth day. Maha Shivaratri in February or March, Skanda Sashti in October or November and Vinayaka Chaturthi are observed with devotion, and the monthly full-moon and Kiruthigai days bring steady crowds. The dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally before you plan a visit.
sections.experience: Many come to Thiruvanmiyur carrying an illness, their own or a loved one's, and pray to the Lord of Medicine for health and peace of mind. If you arrive by bus, you will enter by the western gopuram, steps from the busy coastal road, and the noise falls away as you pass under it. Take a quiet moment near the Vanni tree, walk to the shrine of Valmiki, and look for the carved pillars of the mandapam, before coming to the west-facing linga and then the goddess Tripurasundari. Mornings are calmest; in the evening the temple and its tank fill with families from the neighbourhood, and the old shrine feels very much a living part of the city.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning until around midday and again from late afternoon until about nine in the evening; published timings differ, so confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is in Thiruvanmiyur, on the East Coast Road in south Chennai, with its western gopuram beside the Thiruvanmiyur bus terminus. Many city buses stop here, a suburban railway station serves the neighbourhood, and Chennai International Airport is about 17 km away. Autorickshaws and cabs are easily found.
